{{Short description|American atmospheric scientist}}
'''David Battisti''' (born 1956) is The Tamaki Endowed Chair of [[Atmospheric Sciences]] of the [[University of Washington]] and a fellow at the [[American Geophysical Union]]. His research interests include understanding how interactions between the ocean, land, atmosphere, and sea ice lead to [[climatic variability]] at timescales that vary from seasonal to decadal timescales,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.carnegie-trust.org/news/climate-change-and-global-food-security-professor-david-battisti.html|title=Climate Change and Global Food Security, Professor David Battisti|publisher=Carnegie Trust|accessdate=22 April 2015}}</ref> as well as the [[paleoclimate]]. He is also interested in how climate variability (including [[El Nino]]) affects [[Effects of climate change on agriculture|food production]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/uw-climate-scientist-warms-to-work-on-food-supply/|title=UW climate scientist warms to work on food supply |date=8 December 2009|work=Seattle Times|accessdate=22 April 2015}}</ref>

He received his PhD in 1988 at the University of Washington Department of Atmospheric Sciences.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.atmos.washington.edu/~david/bio.html|title=David S. Battisti|publisher=University of Washington|accessdate=22 April 2015}}</ref> He has published over 100 papers in peer-reviewed journals in atmospheric sciences and [[oceanography]].

He also helps organize an annual set of climate dynamics courses.<ref>[http://www.uib.no/en/rs/acdc Advanced Climate Dynamics Courses]</ref>

Battisti won the [[Carl-Gustaf Rossby Research Medal]] from the [[American Meteorological Society]] in 2021, for his "contributions to understanding climate variability for phenomena ranging from the El Niño/Southern Oscillation and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation to paleoclimate."<ref name = "RossbyMedal"/>
